newsitem.title: FRANCE: Elf says Leuna allegations without foundation.
newsitem.headline: Elf says Leuna allegations without foundation.

text.p: French oil group Elf Aquitaine SA said on Thursday that allegations it had overstated the costs of the Leuna refinery to get higher subsidies were without any foundation.
The oil giant made the statement a day after the European Union said it was starting a probe into the refinery project in eastern Germany.
On Thursday, the European Commission said it had given the German authorities a month to clarify whether Elf received excessive subsidies.
German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said he regretted the matter, which was fueled by German newspaper reports Elf could have inflated the building costs by some one billion marks.
Elf denies these reports. It said the EU probe revived "the discussions that took place in 1996 between the BvS and Elf on the real cost of this refinery."
The BvS, Bundesanstalt fuer Vereinigungsbedingte Sonderaufgaben, is the successor to the Treuhandanstalt body which sold former East German state assets.

"The debate occurred during the preliminary phase of commercial discussions associated with exercising by Elf of its option to sell a 33 percent interest in Mider (the owner and operator of the Leuna refinery) to BvS," Elf said.
The debate centred on a comparison of real costs for the construction, paid by Elf, and a theoretical evaluation of costs for similar units established on statistical bases.

"This valuation, realized for BvS by a consultant whose speciailty -- according to his own acknowledgment -- on the construction engineering was the object of corrections and updating and the disparity between the reality and the estimation was identified by the different parties," Elf said.
"Elf confirms one again that the investment sum which was established with the aid of the best specialised engineering companies, both French and German, corresponds with reality," it said.

"In these circumstances, the allegations relative to an over estimation of the investments in order to increase the subsidy amounts obtained from the German authorities is without foundation," the company said.
Elf added that the Magdenbourg court, which questioned the company on the matter in April 1996, had closed an inquiry after finding no fraud.

The Leuna refinery is due on stream in Autumn 1997. Its total cost was 4.9 billion marks with some German newspapers saying the cost was one billion less. Elf financed 3.5 billion marks and received 1.4 billion in subsidies.

Elf bought the Leuna site in 1992, at the time it was still a state-owned group and headed by chairman Loik Le Floch Prigent who is currently under judicial investigation into his handling of company funds.

In 1994, Treuhand allowed Elf a put option to sell 33 percent in Mitteldeutsche Raffineriegesellschaft (Mider) after the 1997 completion. Treuhand sold the option to Buna Sow Leuna Olefinverbund GmbH (BSL) but when this company was privatised new owner Dow Chemical Co did not want to assume the option.
In August 1996, the European Union said investigators had found no proof of fraud with the subsidies involved.
Rexrodt had asked Elf in May 1996 to justify a difference of some 800 to 900 million marks between the real costs of Leuna and the estimated costs.
The Leuna 2000 project will turn the site into a modern refinery and chemical site with a throughput of 8.7 million tonnes per year of oil and 700,000 tonnes per year of Naphtha.
The complex is being built by a Franco-German consortium of Thyssen, Lurgi and Technip.

It is the first new refinery to be built in Europe for 20 years and comes on stream at a time of overcapacity on the European refinery market and when oil majors are seeking ways to rationalise the industry by closing sites in Britain and France.
